change_log: XenoZeroSignalQuest 1.4.0 — quest logic and visual continuity fixes
success_text:
When you returned to the planet <FromPlanet>, the official of the Orbital Tranquility Office met you with the same smile that is usually attached to invoices for services rendered long ago.
- X-morph? - he asked. - Impossible. The waybill clearly says: "xylomorph, decorative wood form". The storekeeper probably confused a letter or two. He has already been found, promoted and transferred to where he can't harm old documents.
You put a copy of protocol 9-3-7 in front of him, along with a recording in which you are called field subject No. 19.
- Nine-three-seven is a page number in the ventilation manual, - the official immediately explained. - And subject No. 19 is a grille. A very temperamental grille. Its bearing used to whistle, too.
After you demonstrated the station's logs, his smile became thinner, while the sum in the payment window became noticeably thicker. <Money> cr was transferred to your account, including compensation for stress, acid rain and voluntary non-disclosure of what you were going to disclose anyway.
- The culprit has been conclusively identified, - the official announced in parting. - It's the printer. It printed warnings in too small a font. All the best, ranger. And if something suddenly rustles in your hold - don't contact us, contact the department of decorative gardening.
task_text:
Of course we have an assignment for you, ranger <Ranger>. Formally, though, it is considered not an assignment but an inspection of property in working order, so in case of unforeseen circumstances we kindly ask you not to circumstance unforeseenly.
In the <ToStar> system, in orbit of the inhabited planet <ToPlanet>, lies the science-and-cargo station "Nostrom-13". The station belongs to the esteemed interstellar company "Weyland-Yu-Tyani" and has not transmitted either routine reports or a distress signal for eighteen days. The latter especially delights the accounting department: no distress signal means that formally there is no distress. And accounting, ranger, is only ever wrong in favor of accounting.
You need to arrive on the planet <ToPlanet> by <Date>, use the corporate shuttle "Sulaco-2" waiting at the spaceport, check the relay and bring back the station's black box. If you meet the crew, tell them that their reporting delay has reached indecent proportions. If you don't meet the crew, tell us. And one more small thing: cryo-storage D-9 is not recommended to open. It contains... decorative biological materials. Very decorative and completely harmless as long as they remain behind a closed door.
The work pays <Money> cr. The contract is standard, except for appendices seven through nineteen, printed in an especially small font. Do you agree, ranger? It is desirable to decide now.

texts.text:
The spaceport of the planet <ToPlanet> greeted you with the honest bustle of an inhabited world: loaders lost containers, dispatchers found the guilty, and passengers vainly tried to understand why the landing fee had gone up again. By the far wall of the hangar stood a representative of "Weyland-Yu-Tyani" in a gray suit holding three sealed suitcases. Seeing the ranger's ID, he exhaled in relief and handed you a tablet that, instead of a greeting, glowed with: "Subject has arrived".
- A typo, - the representative said hastily. - It should say "specialist". Choose a kit, sign here, here and on the back of your own conscience. "Sulaco-2" has already been refueled. Control is fully automatic - the company considers manual control the cause of most human errors and all maloq errors without exception.
Beyond the transparent wall of the hangar, scheduled shuttles drifted by, dispatchers argued over the landing circles, and the loudspeaker for the third time asked the owner of a blue maloq critter to stop feeding his pet luggage tags. Against the backdrop of the planet's ordinary life, the representative with three identical suitcases looked like the only truly suspicious detail.

The engineering suitcase turned out heavier than the client's promises. Inside lay a laser cutter, a universal fuse, a coil of cable and a manual, "How Not to Die from Electricity in Eleven Simple Steps". The eleventh page was missing. On the other hand, the cutter was charged, and the fuse looked like it had survived only two wars and one scheduled inspection.
On the inside of the suitcase lid someone had scratched a list of previous owners. After two surnames stood the same note: "returned". After the third was written: "kit returned separately". The representative noticed your look and explained that the company values property regardless of the temporary condition of the employee.

The security suitcase held a pulse pistol, two charge cartridges and a form obliging the shooter not to point the weapon at employees, visitors, company property or biological assets. After excluding all the listed targets, shooting was permitted only at the ceiling. You carefully folded the form into your pocket: thick paper sometimes saves you from shrapnel.
The cartridges were of different years of manufacture, but both had passed inspection with the signature of the same inspector. The holster bore a sticker: "Not a means of settling labor disputes". Judging by the soot marks, the previous owner preferred a broad interpretation of the internal rules.

The research kit contained a biosensor, a first-aid kit and a sealed packet with a brochure, "Unknown Life: First Photograph It, Then Run". The scanner was old but working; the first-aid kit was new but already opened by someone. The representative assured you that the missing bandage had been written off on form B-12 and therefore effectively exists.
The biosensor recognized two hundred and forty species of safe mold and one species of dangerous one, marked simply with a question mark. Someone else's setting remained in memory: upon detecting unknown protein mass the device was supposed not to sound an alarm but to vibrate quietly - probably so the specimen wouldn't be the first to get scared.

"Sulaco-2" turned out to be a corporate shuttle of the breed that looks reliable on the outside and on the inside explains why the warranty ended yesterday. The cabin smelled of plastic, ozone and cheap coffee. The autopilot greeted you in the voice of a tired secretary, closed the hatches and demanded that you confirm the voluntary nature of the flight. There was no "do not confirm" button on the panel.
A line flashed in the cargo manifest, "X-121, live culture", but the screen immediately switched to the weather forecast. A cloudless night and local precipitation of decommissioned equipment were expected over the orbit.
Beyond the porthole the spaceport went on living: technicians exchanged gestures, a tug hauled a passenger liner, on the neighboring pad a peleng haggled with a refueling machine. Then the hangar doors closed, the familiar hum vanished, and your cabin became a small hermetically sealed appendix to an overly long corporate contract.

You reached the service menu. Most items were locked behind a corporate password, but the flight log preserved an unusual detail: "Sulaco-2" had made trips to "Nostrom-13" even after the official termination of communications. The last trip delivered there six cryo-containers, two sets of chains and a synthetic consultant of the ASH series. No return cargo was listed.
Another oddity turned up in the maintenance log: before each trip to the station, the entry on the shuttle's mass after its return was deleted from the system. The last mechanic left a pictogram of an open umbrella instead of a signature. The corporate classifier translated it as "precipitation of biological origin" and closed the ticket.

The station grew out of the darkness slowly, as if not approaching but remembering what it looks like. The rings of "Nostrom-13" were not rotating. The navigation lights were silent, the windows dark, the antenna truss frozen at a wrong angle. Not a single welcome pulse, not a single automatic complaint about your course.
The autopilot ignored the demand to stop and steered the shuttle toward the service airlock. For a moment the message "Surveillance channel established" appeared on the screen, then was replaced by a friendlier one: "Welcome, subject No. 19".
The planet <ToPlanet> remained below, bright and populated: cities glimmered on the night side, trade routes ran through orbit. The nearest patrol was less than an hour's flight away, but "Sulaco-2" would not let you open a public channel. Life was right nearby - only the route to it no longer belonged to you.

Docking ended with three impacts: the first of the shuttle against the clamp, the second of the clamp against the station, the third of your head against a panel mounted too low. "Sulaco-2" shut off the engines and reported that the docking locks had been handed to an external operator. The external operator did not respond.
Beyond the station's inner hatch there was vacuum. The manual panel offered to equalize the pressure, but three valves were labeled only with colored circles. Next to them someone had scratched: "Blue first. Don't touch red at zero. Green - after two divisions".
While the automation checked the airtight seal, something lightly ran along the outer hull from the shuttle's nose to its stern. The sensors called it thermal deformation, although metal doesn't usually pause in front of every porthole. Then the sound vanished at the cargo hatch, and the inner lock briefly showed someone else's access command.

A diagram turned up under a decorative panel. The blue valve fed air into the adapter, the green one equalized the pressure with the station, the red one opened the external vent. The correct sequence looked obvious: blue up to two divisions, green until equilibrium, and only then lock the red. But beside the red lever someone had left a fresh print of a clawed limb covered in dried slime.
The temperature drops noticeably near the walls, covered with a thin layer of frost, but the middle of the room remains unpleasantly warm. The automation keeps a log, but instead of the operators' names it puts dashes and one repeating number of the observed subject. Courage helps you take a step. Professionalism reminds you to first look where exactly you are being invited to take it. The automatic voice wishes you a pleasant shift and doesn't specify to whom.

Air entered the adapter with a low howl. The readings stabilized, the inner hatch shuddered and slid aside. Beyond it began a narrow corridor where emergency lamps barely lit the streaks of condensation. The floor was covered with dust, but down the middle ran a clean winding path, as though something large regularly dragged a heavy tail here.
The shuttle behind your back closed automatically. When you tried to open it, the panel replied: "Return permitted after completion of the observation program".
From the service speaker half a note of the corporate anthem sometimes escapes, after which the system prudently falls silent again. On the station diagram this compartment is marked as a warehouse, although the thickness of the walls, the airlocks and the separate power supply suit a quarantine block better. The onboard log calls the situation controlled. That usually means control exists, but is not at all in the hands of the personnel. The accident-free days counter shows eighteen and is clearly proud of its own interpretation.

The cutter went through the casing like a hot knife through a frozen tube of synthetic porridge. You had to sacrifice some air and slightly scorch a sleeve, but the internal drive released the hatch. The station greeted you with darkness, the smell of metal and a long trail on the dusty floor. "Sulaco-2" immediately locked itself from the outside, as if shy of further acquaintance.
Glass from broken indicators crunches underfoot; not a single shard lies where a blow should have thrown it. The fire suppression system has been switched to specimen preservation mode: it has been ordered to cool property before saving personnel. Even a working door seems suspicious when everything else around is broken. Especially if it is locked from the side of an empty room. In the corner a green sign blinks: the object is still considered conditionally safe.

In the reception bay hung a poster: "Nostrom-13 - a safe station for safe science". Under the word "safe" darkened a breach whose edges had been melted from the inside. The duty desk was empty. On it lay a mug of dried-up coffee and a motion sensor that was switched on. The sensor's screen stayed silent exactly until you picked the device up. Then at the very edge of the grid a lone signal appeared and slowly crept toward the center.
Somewhere in the pipes a liquid rolls, and every turn of its flow sounds like cautious movement behind the next door. Spare filters have been unpacked, although the resource counter shows zero hours. Someone was preparing to breathe for a long time, and not through the common system. If the crew left a greeting here, it is composed of open doors, abandoned tools and very expressive traces of haste. The evacuation roster is closed with a signature: those who have left the station are asked to return their passes.

The central corridor diverged in six rays. The signs promised a control room, a living quarter, a medical block, a cargo tier, an engineering deck and laboratories. Half the labels were dark; the other half claimed that all directions were temporarily closed for maintenance. From the ventilation came an occasional metallic tapping. It did not resemble a malfunction: malfunctions usually don't fall silent when you listen to them.
The sensor showed one large moving mark. For now, one.
Static electricity raises the nap on your gloves, and the instruments for a moment show every possible failure at once. The cable channels have been opened from the inside. There are no tooth marks on the insulation, but there are parallel grooves, like the work of claws. You leave a small mark on the wall. If it disappears, there will be proof; if not, at least a landmark. The instructions forbid panic without prior approval from the head of the laboratory.

The control room doors had stopped a palm's width from each other. Beyond them were visible rows of chairs, flickering monitors and a panoramic window with motionless stars. On the floor lay a communications headset; a thin cable vanished into a ventilation grille, and the grille itself was bent outward.
A greasy moisture beads on the metal, resembling neither water nor any technical fluid known on the station. Under a layer of soot a sign of urgent repair is visible. Beside it someone has added by hand that the urgency is canceled until the end of the experiment. You try to move so that the station makes noise, not you. The station, it seems, follows the same tactic. The corporate memo nearby assures that safety begins with trust in the instructions.

The main console was running on emergency power. The system demanded that seven energy units be distributed among life support, doors, communications and surveillance. Ten were required for stable operation. You could temporarily switch on any set of systems, but every extra attempt risked overloading the old distributor.
In the lower corner an unread telemetry packet blinked, addressed simultaneously to "Weyland-Yu-Tyani" and the Orbital Tranquility Office.
It smells of overheated insulation; the smell grows stronger and then vanishes, as though the source were slowly circling the room. One of the bolts has been sheared exactly along the thread. Such force requires a hydraulic tool or an organism with extremely convincing motivation. The Orbital Tranquility Office called this a relay check. The relay is so far the only one behaving decently. A plaque promises a bonus for vigilance, but the recipient's box is prudently left empty.

The distributor diagram resembled a puzzle devised by an engineer in a bad mood. Life support needed three units, the doors - two, communications - four, surveillance - one. On the back of the panel a pencil hint survived: "Surveillance is powered separately. Don't switch on communications together with emergency heating - bus B melts".
The engineering section might hold an auxiliary battery. But you still had to get there.
The weak gravity changes in jerks, making small debris hop up and freeze again in an unnatural order. The inventory lists an extra pressurized container. Its mass changed after every shift, but the remarks were automatically closed by protocol 9-3-7. Every part you find makes the incident clearer and at the same time lessens the wish to meet those who arranged all this. On a faded poster a happy shift thanks the company for the absence of incidents.

You switched off the decorative lighting, the company advertising and the vending machine with diet nuts. The freed-up energy was enough to stabilize the doors and sensors. Somewhere deep in the station actuators came to life. Almost at once the motion sensor beeped: the single mark sharply changed direction and was now moving toward the central tier.
Behind the thick viewing glass the motionless stars look calmer than they should next to so many safety violations. The surveillance camera is turned toward the ceiling and still warm, as if someone had recently not wanted to end up in the corporate archive. The station seems to suggest hurrying, but it was precisely the hurried ones here who, judging by the traces, were served faster and more finally than the rest. The onboard network offers to rate the quality of service on a five-point scale.

The surveillance grid combined the data from the pressure, heat and motion sensors. The target moved through the technical tunnels faster than a human, at times vanished near the cooling mains and radiated almost no heat. It reacted not to light but to sharp air fluctuations and noise.
On the camera recording a long black silhouette flashed. The frame ended where the creature turned its smooth head straight toward the lens.
Behind the bulkheads cooling metal taps quietly, as though the station were counting seconds to an event it forgot to warn about. The portable terminal catches a service telemetry packet, poorly encrypted but sent outward with exemplary regularity. The contract surely had a clause on natural wear and tear of the ranger, but now it is especially pleasant that you didn't finish reading it. The system politely asks that violations be reported to the very employee who committed them.

The transmitter was in working order, but its emergency channel had been physically disconnected from the antenna. The connector lay nearby, neatly wrapped in a seal: "Do not connect until completion of field trials". This was not a consequence of an attack. Someone had made sure in advance that the station could not call for help.
The light here comes in short blue flashes; between them the corridor manages to become deeper and, it seems, a bit narrower. In the memory of the nearest controller there is an empty gap of exactly eighteen days - too neat for an ordinary malfunction. A ranger's intuition isn't mystical: it is simply the memory of many situations where the most harmless hatch opened last. The company slogan reminds: any result is valuable if the report is composed correctly.

After you connected the plug, the terminal dumped the queue of undelivered messages. The last was sent by the captain: "If anyone is reading this, the company knew. They brought eggs. ASH sealed the airlocks. In the central shaft so far only one adult specimen". An automatic reply from the Office followed: "Message received. Continue observation. A rescue operation is economically inexpedient".
The air holds the smell of ozone, old lubricant and the sterile compound with which someone else's panic was unsuccessfully scrubbed away. There are fresh scratches on the service panel: the cover was opened not with a tool but with something narrow, hard and very strong. The good news is that the equipment still works. The bad news is that it clearly doesn't work for your convenience. The warranty seal is intact; whatever was under it vanished much earlier.

The camera archive preserved the crew's last hours. People dragged containers to the laboratory, while the synthetic ASH-8 watched them with motionless politeness. Then one container opened. The camera went dark, but the sound continued for four more minutes.
In a service line you found the first fragment of the escape pod code: the digit 4. Evidently someone was trying to leave a route for those who would come after.
A faint tremor runs through the decking, although the station's engines are silent and not a single pump is listed as running. Next to the door is stuck an evacuation checklist: all boxes filled in advance, including the signature of a person who disappeared a week earlier. You mentally add one more item to the future bill. The list is already longer than the official assignment and considerably more truthful. The emergency regulations begin with advice to remain calm and keep a backup copy.

The living quarter met you with many open doors and a silence too neat for panic. Personal belongings remained in place: shoes, photographs, board games, half-empty glasses. Only the mattresses had been torn from the beds and dragged to the ventilation shafts. On the wall someone had written: "Don't make noise. It hears".
The ventilation exhales in portions: a long whistle, a pause, then a wet click somewhere very near the grille. The door's manual drive has been lubricated recently. There are no fingerprints on the handle, only a transparent film and the smell of strong alkali. You mark the way back. On a normal station that is caution; on this one it is also an optimistic assumption that the way will remain. The automatic voice wishes you a pleasant shift and doesn't specify to whom.

The captain's cabin was locked from the inside. In the desk lay a paper logbook - a rare luxury on a modern station and excellent protection against corporate data deletion. The captain wrote that the laboratory code is assembled from the numbers of four shifts: captain, engineer, doctor, cargo master. His own shift was the first.
The last entry ended with the words: "ASH claims that the rescuers are already on their way. ASH never blinks when he lies. Then again, he doesn't blink at all".
Condensation gathers on the ceiling in large drops and falls with such regularity that you involuntarily begin to wait for a missed one. The emergency beacon is physically intact, but its antenna is switched to a closed corporate channel with priority for hidden telemetry. There are too many signs of struggle here for an accident and too few coincidences for an honest investigation. An unpleasant third option remains. The accident-free days counter shows eighteen and is clearly proud of its own interpretation.

The engineer's place had that special order in which the owner knows the location of every nut, and an outsider risks dying under an avalanche of tools. A note survived in the tablet: "My shift is the third, but in the code I come after the captain". Beside it lay a scorched pass and a diagram of the auxiliary battery.
On the back of the diagram the engineer had added: "If the laboratory doors jam again, cut to the left of the emblem. To the right runs a pipe with something they pay more for than for us".
The emergency lamps light the dust from below, turning ordinary cables into moving silhouettes with excessively long limbs. The equipment markings have been neatly covered with new corporate labels; the old numbers beneath them belong to a military biolab. Experience suggests: when the client calls such a thing a trifle, the trifle usually knows how to run on the ceiling and does not recognize warranty obligations. In the corner a green sign blinks: the object is still considered conditionally safe.

The doctor kept an audio diary. At first the voice was calm: "Specimen X-121 demonstrates an unusual growth rate". Then irritated: "The corporation has forbidden destroying the clutch". The last entry sounded in a whisper: "My shift is the second. In the code I'm third. The creature has acid instead of blood. Do not shoot near the hull".
The silence isn't complete: in it you can hear your own breathing, the rustle of fabric and a distant sound, too soft for a mechanism. The pressure sensor is in working order, but its alarm output has been physically unsoldered from the transmitter; coincidence is smelled here more faintly than solder flux. The company clearly economized on people but not on surveillance equipment. So seeing what was happening mattered more to it than stopping it. The evacuation roster is closed with a signature: those who have left the station are asked to return their passes.

The cargo master's cabin had been ransacked. In the closet you found half a protective suit, a cassette of emergency oxygen and an inscription on the door: "I am the fourth. If you reach the pod, the first digit of the launch is four". Under the bed lay a token with shift number 7 - the last element of the laboratory code.
The temperature drops noticeably near the walls, covered with a thin layer of frost, but the middle of the room remains unpleasantly warm. The pipeline is duplicated by a hidden line that is absent from the civilian documentation; it goes down, toward the laboratory tier. When it is all over, the official will certainly call this an unforeseen feature of the facility. You prepare a foreseen answer in advance. The instructions forbid panic without prior approval from the head of the laboratory.

The collected records formed a sequence: captain - 1, engineer - 3, doctor - 2, cargo master - 7. Laboratory code: 1327. Too simple for a secret complex, but quite fitting for an institution where the password to the archives was stuck to the monitor with a note "do not remove".
From the service speaker half a note of the corporate anthem sometimes escapes, after which the system prudently falls silent again. A yellow line of the safe route is painted on the floor; it unexpectedly ends at a ventilation shaft and continues nowhere else. Just in case, you memorize the location of the nearest airlock, the fire extinguisher, and an object that could be convincingly thrown in the other direction. The corporate memo nearby assures that safety begins with trust in the instructions.

The food machine in the canteen was still working. It offered soup, tea and a "protein composition with the taste of memories of meat". Scratches ran across the floor, and under the table lay a broken sensor. In its memory a short route of the creature was preserved: it more often chose dark passages and retreated from jets of emergency coolant.
Glass from broken indicators crunches underfoot; not a single shard lies where a blow should have thrown it. The automation keeps a log, but instead of the operators' names it puts dashes and one repeating number of the observed subject. You listen once more and decide to treat the absence of an answer not as silence but as an evasive remark from the station. A plaque promises a bonus for vigilance, but the recipient's box is prudently left empty.

Through the viewing window half the station and the bluish disk of the planet <ToPlanet> were visible. Dozens of palm prints were imprinted on the glass from the inside. Among them were marks unlike any hand you knew. Under the window lay a child's drawing sent to one of the technicians: a station, stars and the caption "Daddy, come back". A corporate stamp over the drawing announced: "The return of the employee is not provided for by the contract".
Somewhere in the pipes a liquid rolls, and every turn of its flow sounds like cautious movement behind the next door. On the station diagram this compartment is marked as a warehouse, although the thickness of the walls, the airlocks and the separate power supply suit a quarantine block better. You check your helmet fastenings and remember that hazard pay always sounds more solid before you meet the hazard itself. On a faded poster a happy shift thanks the company for the absence of incidents.

The medical block door opened with a belated sterility signal. Inside it smelled of antiseptic and something sweetish and rotten. On one cot lay a crew member, strapped down with belts. The chest had been torn open from the inside. Above the cot a diagnosis continued to blink: "Food poisoning. Rest recommended".
Static electricity raises the nap on your gloves, and the instruments for a moment show every possible failure at once. The fire suppression system has been switched to specimen preservation mode: it has been ordered to cool property before saving personnel. The longer the inspection lasts, the clearer it becomes: what should have been paid for was not the delivery of the black box but your silence after it. The onboard network offers to rate the quality of service on a five-point scale.

Marks on the belts showed that the person had been held deliberately. The video recording of the procedure had been deleted, but the biosensor could restore part of the readings. In the wound remained microscopic particles of a substance that burned through surgical steel and at the same time curdled its own tissues, not letting the blood drain out completely.
A greasy moisture beads on the metal, resembling neither water nor any technical fluid known on the station. Spare filters have been unpacked, although the resource counter shows zero hours. Someone was preparing to breathe for a long time, and not through the common system. Some problems are solved with weapons. This one, for now, suggests thinking first - a rare courtesy that is best taken advantage of. The system politely asks that violations be reported to the very employee who committed them.

You used the remote manipulators. The scanner confirmed: the blood of an adult specimen is concentrated acid; the body is protected by internal neutralizing membranes. Fire and deep cooling should slow the reaction. Killing such a creature in a cramped corridor is possible, but the result risks burning through the floor, the ceiling and the careless victor along with it.
It smells of overheated insulation; the smell grows stronger and then vanishes, as though the source were slowly circling the room. The cable channels have been opened from the inside. There are no tooth marks on the insulation, but there are parallel grooves, like the work of claws. Courage helps you take a step. Professionalism reminds you to first look where exactly you are being invited to take it. The company slogan reminds: any result is valuable if the report is composed correctly.

The medical cabinet was locked, but beside it lay the doctor's card. Inside were stimulants, an oxygen supply and an ampoule marked "X neutralizer". The ampoule turned out to be empty. Judging by the scratches, someone had been in a great hurry to find that out before you.
The weak gravity changes in jerks, making small debris hop up and freeze again in an unnatural order. Under a layer of soot a sign of urgent repair is visible. Beside it someone has added by hand that the urgency is canceled until the end of the experiment. The onboard log calls the situation controlled. That usually means control exists, but is not at all in the hands of the personnel. The warranty seal is intact; whatever was under it vanished much earlier.

In a side laboratory stood jars with fragments of a black carapace. The central container had been smashed from the inside. The terminal called the specimen "X-121, perfect organism" and demanded that the crew be assessed not as personnel but as a nutrient medium. Under the document was the electronic signature of the official from the planet <FromPlanet>.
Behind the thick viewing glass the motionless stars look calmer than they should next to so many safety violations. One of the bolts has been sheared exactly along the thread. Such force requires a hydraulic tool or an organism with extremely convincing motivation. Even a working door seems suspicious when everything else around is broken. Especially if it is locked from the side of an empty room. The emergency regulations begin with advice to remain calm and keep a backup copy.

The cargo tier was huge and almost empty. The containers stood open, chains lay on the floor, a loader was pressed against the wall. Water dripped steadily from above. The motion sensor showed the target right behind you, then on the left, then above. In the silence came a short metallic scrape - as if a claw were testing the strength of a ventilation grille.
Behind the bulkheads cooling metal taps quietly, as though the station were counting seconds to an event it forgot to warn about. The inventory lists an extra pressurized container. Its mass changed after every shift, but the remarks were automatically closed by protocol 9-3-7. If the crew left a greeting here, it is composed of open doors, abandoned tools and very expressive traces of haste. The automatic voice wishes you a pleasant shift and doesn't specify to whom.

The creature descended without a sound. First a long smooth skull appeared, then a narrow body glistening with condensation. It was taller than a human but held itself hunched, as though the whole corridor seemed too cramped for it. The jaws parted, and a second mouth appeared inside.
The hunter did not lunge at once. It listened. One adult X-morph, one ranger and too many ways to make a wrong move.
The sensor confirmed what you saw with stubborn precision: one adult target, distance twelve meters, speed zero. But the creature's tail slowly traced a semicircle on the floor, cutting off the way back. It was not merely waiting for movement - it was choosing where you would run when you finally broke from your spot.

You slipped into a service cabinet and pulled the door to. The creature passed close by, scraping its tail along the metal. Through the crack you could see it stopping beside every vibrating pipe. The motion sensor uselessly beeped in your palm. You had to clamp the speaker with your fingers and wait until the mark moved away.
Every touch of the claws carried through the thin metal. The hunter lingered at the little door, drew air in between its teeth and slowly moved on. You counted the intervals between the tail strikes until they dissolved in the noise of the ventilation, and only then allowed yourself to breathe fully.

The first pulse hit the carapace and threw the creature back against the containers. It shrieked, but rose at once. The second shot made it retreat into the ventilation. Smoking drops remained on the floor, burning through the decking down to the cable channel. The hunter was wounded, angry and now knew your scent for certain.
The acid kept hissing in the breach, eating the decking layer by layer. On the lower deck a leak sensor tripped, and a jet of neutralizer stopped the reaction a few centimeters from a power cable. Another successful shot from that distance could have beaten the creature and at the same time shut down half the station.

You set the loader to idle and aimed it at the open cargo airlock. The rumbling machine interested the creature more than live prey. When the long head appeared between the containers, you laid your palm on the emergency grate button. One more moment - and the hunter's tail would be entirely inside the capture zone.
The loader crawled toward the airlock agonizingly slowly, clanging in every joint. The creature kept behind the containers and moved parallel to the lure; at times only the smooth top of its skull showed above the crates. Two steps remained to the grate button, and both had to be made before the hunter realized the substitution.

The airlock held. A crack slowly appeared on the viewing glass, and from the darkness behind it a smooth black skull looked at you. The creature neither thrashed about nor wasted strength. It simply waited for the machinery to give way. The behavior was far too calculating for a "decorative wood form".
The grate mechanism creaked in protest, the resource indicator dropped with every blow. But the motion sensor finally showed the target in a fixed sector. You gained a few minutes of freedom and an important piece of knowledge: X-121 can be outwitted, but it probably won't fall for the same trick a second time.

The creature went into the ventilation, leaving a streak of acid on the grate. You hadn't beaten it, but you had won time. The sensor showed a faint mark moving toward the lower laboratories. It became quiet in the cargo bay - and precisely because of that a rustle clearly came from under one container.
Behind the ventilation grille a fast, receding scratching could still be heard. The wounded target vanished from the sensors near the cold pipes and reappeared where the shafts opened onto the central tier. Now the hunter was not merely looking for prey - it was memorizing your route and choosing a place for the next meeting.

Beyond the transparent segment of the tunnel the planet <ToPlanet> slowly rotated, huge, near and for now completely unreachable.

The suit held pressure, but the oxygen reserve was calculated for twenty minutes of calm work. Calm work did not include fleeing from creatures able to move along the outer hull. You could move slowly and sparingly or dash for the capsule, spending air.
You checked the neck ring, the gloves and the emergency tank twice. The third time, from the outer darkness a silhouette with a long tail crawled across the glass, needing neither air nor a safety line. After that, saving oxygen became psychologically harder, but the direction of movement stopped raising doubts.

The capsule console required three digits. The collected hints gave 4-8-1. The biosensor could reconstruct the code from traces on the keys, and ASH-8's service key could bypass the check. A mistake triggered a purge of the tunnel and the launch of the capsule without a passenger.
Frost covered the edges of the keys, and the thick gloves turned every press into a separate operation. Beyond the outer glass something for a moment blocked out the stars and vanished behind the capsule's hull. The console patiently waited for three digits, not sharing your interest in entering them on the first try.

The capsule tore from its guides and entered the atmosphere of the planet <ToPlanet>. Through the small porthole you could see the station and dark figures crawling along its outer ring. Navigation worked, the parachute promised to deploy, and the corporate beacon was already transmitting that the capsule was lost along with its contents. For the first time you fully agreed with a corporate report.
The g-force pressed you into the seat, the fastenings creaked, and the station instantly shrank into a dark diagram beyond the porthole. The autopilot chose a landing corridor between civilian routes and honestly warned that the landing accuracy was plus or minus two hundred kilometers. After D-9 that sounded almost caring.

The capsule landed in a salt marsh two hundred kilometers from the spaceport. They found you by your cursing sooner than by the beacon. Most of the equipment stayed on the station, but a copy of the main log was preserved in the suit's memory. You climbed out, which means that on the planet <FromPlanet> someone would have to very diligently pretend to be surprised.

The reactor was under the lair. Overloading it would destroy the queen, the clutch and most of the evidence. Therefore the archive had to be sent out first. The antenna worked in fits, and the observers were already trying to close access. ASH-8, if freed from the protocol, offered to hold the channel. If not, it would have to be done by hand.
The silence isn't complete: in it you can hear your own breathing, the rustle of fabric and a distant sound, too soft for a mechanism. The surveillance camera is turned toward the ceiling and still warm, as if someone had recently not wanted to end up in the corporate archive. Experience suggests: when the client calls such a thing a trifle, the trifle usually knows how to run on the ceiling and does not recognize warranty obligations. A plaque promises a bonus for vigilance, but the recipient's box is prudently left empty.

The archive went out in three packets: the crew's logs, protocol 9-3-7 and the "subject No. 19" recording. "Weyland-Yu-Tyani" tried to recall the data, but you had sent copies to the Rangers Center, two newspapers and a cooking forum - the only place where corporate censorship had no authority.
The temperature drops noticeably near the walls, covered with a thin layer of frost, but the middle of the room remains unpleasantly warm. The portable terminal catches a service telemetry packet, poorly encrypted but sent outward with exemplary regularity. The company clearly economized on people but not on surveillance equipment. So seeing what was happening mattered more to it than stopping it. On a faded poster a happy shift thanks the company for the absence of incidents.

The reactor hall was flooded with red emergency light. Three control rods required a sequence: remove cooling, raise the two outer rods and only then the central one. If you raised the central one first, the hall would turn into plasma before you had time to regret the decision.
From the service speaker half a note of the corporate anthem sometimes escapes, after which the system prudently falls silent again. In the memory of the nearest controller there is an empty gap of exactly eighteen days - too neat for an ordinary malfunction. When it is all over, the official will certainly call this an unforeseen feature of the facility. You prepare a foreseen answer in advance. The onboard network offers to rate the quality of service on a five-point scale.

The rods came out of the active zone. The siren announced eight turns until the station's destruction and asked the personnel to proceed to the exits without panic. Beyond the doors there was no longer any personnel, but there were plenty of reasons for panic. From the reactor to the outer airlock there was a short way through the lair and a long one through the engineering deck.
Red strips of lighting ran toward the exits, marking the way one after another. At the same time dozens of small signals appeared on the sensor: the clutch had felt the heat of the reactor. Now a wrong turn cost not only time - it allowed the growing swarm to cut off the next section before you could get there.

The first corridor shuddered. Sparks showered from the ceiling, the emergency doors began to close by sections. Behind you young specimens poured from the laboratory tier. Ahead a steam pipe burst; you could wait out the release or dash through it, losing health but gaining time.
Steam blocked the corridor with a white wall. Behind it the young specimens clicked, but the howl of the siren kept them from determining your position. You had to choose between a burn now and an encounter after a delay; the reactor was not interested in the quality of the decision and kept counting seconds with equally loud blows.

The central tier was already on fire. The wounded hunter - if it was still alive - crossed the corridor ahead. The light blinked, and the creature vanished. The direct path to the airlock ran through the control room; the detour added two sections and used up oxygen.
The hunter appeared in the red light and froze for a moment opposite you. An explosion in the neighboring section made it duck, opening a direct way through the control room. The detour was safer only in theory: a crack was already running along the outer wall, and the air supply shrank with every compartment that went dark.

Several dozen meters remained to the outer airlock. The floor was splitting, gravity worked in fits, and beyond the viewing window the sections of the station went dark one after another. The spacesuit hung by the door. Without it you could make it to the shuttle only as a very fast cloud of steam.
The spacesuit tore off its mounting and slowly floated across the corridor when gravity vanished again. You caught it by the sleeve, hit the wall and saw the last door to the airlock begin to close. The timer left exactly enough time to act correctly, with no chance to correct yourself.

The airlock opened straight into space. "Sulaco-2" drifted a hundred meters away, already freed from the clamps by the explosion. Pieces of plating flew between you and the shuttle. The timer showed the last seconds. All that remained was to push off from the station and hope that the trajectory would prove more convincing than a corporate contract.
In the vacuum the siren and the roar of destruction vanished; what remained were flashes, shocks through the soles and the timer digits on your wrist. Debris crossed the space between the airlock and the shuttle at different speeds. There was no safe window - only a short interval in which the danger looked slightly less final.

You pushed off. "Nostrom-13" opened up behind you in white-and-red light, and the shock wave flung you toward the shuttle. The manipulator caught the handrail, your gloves slid, but the safety line held. A few seconds later the station turned into an expanding cloud of metal, ice and finally unprofitable biological assets.
In flight you couldn't speed up or turn, only trust the calculated push. The shuttle grew in the visor too slowly, the station behind you too brightly. The handrail passed right by your glove; the last impulse of the maneuvering unit shifted your palm by a few centimeters and turned a miss into a chance.

"Sulaco-2" reached the planet <ToPlanet> on emergency thrust. A short new star was still visible in the sky - all that remained of "Nostrom-13". The archives had already spread across the network, and the company issued a statement about an unscheduled fireworks display. You had destroyed the lair and gotten out. Now all that remained was to collect the money from a man who surely knew nothing about it.

You returned the suitcase to the representative and left the spaceport. He did not argue - he only noted on the tablet: "Subject declined. Find a more curious one". A few weeks later "Nostrom-13" vanished from the navigation registries. The Office explained this as statistical optimization.

You had the shuttle unlocked before entering the laboratories and flew away without learning the whole truth. "Weyland-Yu-Tyani" thanked you for the partial inspection, refused to pay and sent another specialist to the station. A month later contact was lost with three neighboring ships.

You yanked the red valve at zero pressure. The airlock opened outward, and the air tried to leave the shuttle together with you. Your last thought was surprise: accounting really hadn't exaggerated the risks - it had merely printed them too small.

The jumper flared with white light. Current passed through your gloves, your suit and all your doubts at once. The station got three extra seconds of power, and the experiment a short but convincing record of the conductivity of rangers.

You touched the specimen with a tool. A drop of acid slid along the metal, burned through the table and landed on your sleeve. While you tried to shed your suit, the floor under your feet vanished too. The medical terminal diagnosed mild skin irritation.

The egg's flaps opened with a wet sigh. The pale creature leaped faster than you could raise your hand. A few hours later you woke up surprisingly cheerful, felt hungry - and then someone inside your chest decided it was time for breakfast too.

The sensor beeped in the closed cabinet. The creature stopped, slowly turned its head and punched through the door with its inner jaw. The corporate instruction turned out to be right: electronics in a hiding place really should be switched to silent mode.

You fired almost point-blank. The carapace shattered, but the moment of triumph lasted less than a second: a stream of acid covered you and cut through the decking. Below was another service tier. You reached it before your own remains did.

You bent over the fallen hunter. Its tail twitched one last time, rupturing the acid sac. The heroic pose came out flawless; too bad the observers didn't manage to take a picture before the camera dissolved.

You shorted the contacts by hand. The generator came to life, the station lit up, and for a few moments you became the brightest object on the engineering deck. Then the automation shut off the power upon detecting a foreign conductor.

In the cramped shaft there was no room to turn around. First teeth flashed behind you, then the inner jaw pierced your helmet. The motion sensor kept showing two marks for several more seconds, after which only one remained again.
The third mistake set off the siren. It was so loud that the hunter didn't need a motion sensor. The laboratory door never opened, but the ventilation grille behind your back did - quite readily.

You turned your back on ASH-8. The synthetic politely thanked you for your cooperation and broke your neck with one precise movement. In his report he noted that subject No. 19 had voluntarily ceased participation for medical reasons.

The red valve released toxic coolant into the room. The eggs opened from the heat, and you lost consciousness before the first many-legged shadows reached the console. The cryosystem recorded a successful thawing of biological assets.

You closed the drain with the nitrogen open. The pipe burst, turning shards of ice into shrapnel. The queen roared below, the eggs stirred, and the station logged the accident as a scheduled pressure increase.

You came too close to the egg. The flaps parted, and the creature leaped onto your helmet. It found the edge of the seal faster than you found your emergency knife. The rest of the experiment proceeded strictly according to the corporate plan.

The clutch woke all at once. One facehugger can be knocked away, two can be dodged, but dozens turned the floor into a living wave. The last frame from your camera aroused particularly high scientific interest among the observers.

You decided to attack the queen directly. The chains snapped before her carapace did. The huge head darted forward, the tail knocked the weapon away, and the experiment received rare data on how far a ranger can fly within a single lair.

The shuttle left the station, and you allowed yourself to relax. From the ventilation above your seat a young hunter slowly descended. The autopilot continued the landing on the densely populated planet <ToPlanet>, conscientiously delivering both biological assets.

You entered the airless tunnel without a sealed suit. Only three sections remained to the capsule, but a ranger's body counts distance differently. A minute later the beacon registered a motionless object and suggested it contact the support service.

The wrong code shot the capsule off without you. You followed it with your eyes while a ventilation grille opened behind your back. An empty rescue craft went into space, and in the company's statistics there appeared one successfully evacuated unit of property.

You raised the central rod first. The reactor turned the hall into a small sun without warning, countdown or the possibility of lodging a complaint. "Nostrom-13" vanished quickly, but the ranger - even faster.

The timer reached zero in the central corridor. For a moment the station became transparent with light, then flew apart. The lair was destroyed, the evidence sent, but the bonus would have to be collected by someone considerably less vaporized.

You opened the outer airlock without a spacesuit. The vacuum caught you and carried you toward the shuttle, but there was no one left to assess the accuracy of the trajectory. From a technical standpoint, the escape succeeded about halfway.

A piece of antenna crossed your trajectory. The impact tore the safety line and sent you spinning away from the shuttle. "Nostrom-13" exploded beautifully; too bad you had to watch it for a very long time and with no chance of going back for the money.
